summary:
EcoBits forecasts how vegetation fires will spread, the way weather models forecast a hurricane’s track. Instead of explaining a fire after it is out, it shows where the fire is now, where it will be in 3, 6 and 12 hours, how fast it moves, and when it will reach each village and road.

We fuse NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS and VIIRS and filter out gas flares, factories and offshore platforms, so only real open fires raise alerts. The terrain becomes a graph of 19,500 nodes built from Copernicus elevation, Sentinel-2 vegetation and hourly ERA5 weather. A simplified Rothermel-style model sets the spread rate in each cell from wind, slope, fuel and moisture, and Dijkstra’s algorithm finds when fire reaches each cell. Forty scenarios run in parallel to measure uncertainty, restarting every hour from the latest observed perimeter.

An interactive 3D map shows the results. Our Rescue Operations Plan turns them into safe crew routes, evacuation routes, safe zones and a suppression tactic for each sector. We validated the model on a real 2019 fire in Dhofar. Next, machine learning trained on NASA’s fire history will predict ignition risk.

The goal: civil defense and rescue teams decide based on forecasts, not guesswork.
details:
EcoBits: Predictive Wildfire Intelligence for Oman

What it does
EcoBits forecasts where a vegetation fire will be in the next 3, 6 and 12 hours, the way hurricane models forecast a storm’s track. Most traditional tools explain a fire after it is out. EcoBits looks ahead: it estimates when the fire will reach each village and road, how likely that is, and what crews should do about it. Our pilot area is Jebel Qara in Dhofar, Oman.

How it works

  1. Detect: We fuse NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from four satellites (MODIS, plus VIIRS on S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21). Detections from different sensors within 1 km and 60 minutes are merged into one event. We then filter out false fires: gas flares, factories and offshore platforms. The filter combines NASA’s static-source reference (4,445 cells built from 630,000 detections), 5,351 industrial sites from OpenStreetMap, and recurrence over 7 days. In one 24-hour test over Oman, 175 of 193 thermal events were industrial or offshore, which leaves only the real open fires to raise an alert.
  2. Model: The terrain is a graph of 19,500 nodes and 306,980 directed edges (a 130 × 150 grid, 16 neighbors per node), built from real Copernicus DEM elevation, Sentinel-2 NDVI/NDMI vegetation and hourly ERA5 weather. Dijkstra’s algorithm computes when fire reaches every node. Spread rates follow published fire science: elliptical spread (Anderson 1983), grass curing (Cheney 1998), and Byram fireline intensity and flame length.
  3. Quantify uncertainty: Each forecast runs 40 Monte Carlo scenarios with perturbed wind, fuel and moisture. That is 780,000 node solutions in about 36 ms, restarted every hour from the observed fire perimeter. The output is an arrival-probability map with a P10–P90 arrival-time band, not a single guess.
  4. Decide: An operations plan turns the forecast into action. A time-dependent router keeps crews away from any node the fire could reach first. It suggests a suppression tactic per sector (hand crews, engines, air support or indirect attack) from fire intensity, slope, access and time of day, and adds evacuation routes, safety zones, a suggested command post, LCES checks and a printable briefing.

Scientific rigor
A Science Lab replays historical fires on two synced maps, the observed fire against the simulation. A leakage guard blocks any input from after the start time. We validated the model on a real fire in the Qara mountains (14 January 2019) against a Sentinel-2 dNBR burn scar; model 2 improved overlap (IoU) by about 40% over model 1. We also run Morris sensitivity analysis, Brier-score calibration, the full Canadian Fire Weather Index (matching the reference test case), and 50 unit tests. Every synthetic or estimated layer is labeled as such in the interface.

Impact
Civil defense, rescue teams, officials and nearby residents get decisions based on forecasts instead of guesswork: who to evacuate first, which roads stay safe and for how long, and where to attack the fire.

Tools
JavaScript, HTML/CSS and Python. MapLibre GL (3D terrain and globe), D3.js and three.js. Python with NumPy and Rasterio to build the data. Cloudflare Pages and Pages Functions for hosting and the API. Open data from NASA FIRMS, NASA GIBS (MODIS LST, SMAP), ESA Copernicus (DEM, Sentinel-2), ERA5/Open-Meteo and OpenStreetMap. The interface is bilingual (Arabic/English) and needs no special hardware: it runs in a browser.

What makes it creative
It treats fire spread as a shortest-path problem on a graph, which makes 40 parallel futures cheap enough to recompute every hour. It also connects the whole chain, from a satellite pixel to a route a crew can drive, in one tool.

Factors we considered
Honesty of the data over attractive numbers, false alarms from industrial heat sources, Dhofar’s dry-season grasslands, night operations with no air support, safety of both crews and civilians, and reproducible validation without future data. The model is still in development; next steps are a per-cell wind field and independent validation on more fires.
